_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-02 19:30:04Z)**_

**No — it's small for your machine.**

The folder holds a clone of **Gitea** (the Go/TypeScript self-hosted Git server), plus two lecture PDFs.

| | Size |
|---|---|
| `.git` (history, 290k objects, one pack) | 323 MB |
| Working tree (6,240 source files) | 31 MB |
| **Gitea total** | **354 MB** |
| Lecture PDFs | 10 MB |
| **Folder total** | **~365 MB** |

Your C: drive is 952 GB with **526 GB free** — the repo is about **0.07%** of your free space. Even by repo standards this is only medium-sized; the history dominates because Gitea has ~290k objects going back years, but it's already packed into a single well-compressed packfile, so there's nothing to reclaim with `git gc`.

Two things worth knowing, since neither shows up in that number:

- **Building it will cost much more than cloning it.** Gitea is Go + a pnpm/Vite frontend. `go build` pulls the module cache into `%USERPROFILE%\go\pkg\mod` and `pnpm install` creates a `node_modules/` — together those typically run **1.5–3 GB**. Still fine on 526 GB free, just don't be surprised when the folder and your home directory grow.
- **The path is on your Desktop.** Per your setup notes, `Desktop\Classes` is the local copy, not the OneDrive-synced one — so this isn't currently syncing 6,240 files to the cloud. Worth keeping it that way; a Go/node project inside a OneDrive folder is a reliable source of file-lock and sync-churn pain.

===== AGENTS.md =====
- Use `make help` to find available development targets
- Run `make fmt` to format `.go` files, and run `make lint-go` to lint them
- Run `make lint-js` to lint `.ts` files
- Run `make tidy` after any `go.mod` changes
- Run single go tests with `go test -run '^TestName$' ./modulepath/`
- Run single js test files with `pnpm exec vitest <path-filter>`
- Run single playwright e2e test files with `GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='<filepath>' make test-e2e`
- Add the current year into the copyright header of new `.go` files
- Ensure no trailing whitespace in edited files
- Use Conventional Commits for commit messages and PR titles, e.g. `type(scope): subject`; `!` before the colon if breaking. Use `test` type for test-only changes.
- Never force-push, amend, or squash unless asked. Use new commits and normal push for pull request updates
- Preserve existing code comments, do not remove or rewrite comments that are still relevant
- Keep comments short, prefer same-line, explain why, never narrate code
- Prefer unit tests over integration tests when logic is testable in isolation
- Aim for sub-2s local runtime for integration and e2e tests
- In TypeScript, use `!` (non-null assertion) instead of `?.`/`??` when a value is known to always exist
- For CSS layout, prefer `flex-*` helpers over per-child `tw-ml-*` / `tw-mr-*` margins; fall back to `tw-*` utilities when specificity requires `!important`
- Include authorship attribution in issue and pull request comments
- Always add `Assisted-By` trailers to commit messages in format `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION`
- Never add `Co-Authored-By` `Signed-off-by` trailer to commit messages. Sign off must be done by a human.
```

# Student Guide — Running Gitea Locally

Welcome! This is a course fork of [Gitea](https://about.gitea.com/), a self-hosted Git service
written in **Go** (backend) and **Vue/TypeScript** (frontend). You'll be improving the kind of tool
you use every day — issues, pull requests, code review, CI/Actions.

This guide gets you from a fresh clone to a running Gitea on your machine, backed by **SQLite** (no
separate database server needed). It should take ~15–30 minutes, most of which is the first backend
compile.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

Install these before you start. Versions below are the minimums this fork is pinned to.

| Tool | Version | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Go** | **1.26.4+** | Backend. `go.mod` requires `go 1.26.4`. |
| **Node.js** | **22.18.0+** | Frontend build only (not needed at runtime). |
| **pnpm** | **11.0.0+** | Frontend package manager. Easiest via `corepack enable`. |
| **Git** | 2.x | Required both to build **and at runtime** (Gitea shells out to git). |

> 💡 **New to Go?** Gitea's backend is written in Go. [A Tour of Go](https://go.dev/tour/) is the official interactive tutorial (~2 hours) and covers everything you need for typical backend tasks. Pay attention to goroutines and interfaces — both appear frequently in this codebase.

> 📖 **Developer docs:** [`docs/development.md`](docs/development.md) in this repo covers the development workflow, how to run tests, database migration conventions, and the overall package structure. Read it before picking a task.

**You do NOT need a C compiler (gcc).** This version of Gitea uses a pure-Go SQLite driver
(`modernc.org/sqlite`) and builds with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, so there's no MSYS2/MinGW/Xcode-tools step.
This is the main reason setup is painless on Windows.

**Optional:** `make` (convenience only — every command below also has a no-`make` form), and Docker
(if you'd rather run the official container instead of building).

### Installing the toolchain
- **Windows:** `winget install GoLang.Go` and `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS`, then `corepack enable`.
- **macOS:** `brew install go node` then `corepack enable`.
- **Linux:** use your package manager (or the official Go tarball) for Go + Node, then `corepack enable`.

Verify:
```bash
go version      # go1.26.x
node --version  # v22.18+ (or newer)
pnpm --version  # 11.x
git --version
```

---

## 2. Get the code

```bash
git clone https://github.com/musta55/gitea.git
cd gitea
```

---

## 3. Build

Gitea is built in two halves: the frontend assets (with pnpm/vite) and the backend binary (with Go).

### Option A — with `make` (recommended if you have it)
```bash
make build          # builds frontend + backend into ./gitea (or gitea.exe on Windows)
```

### Option B — without `make` (works everywhere)
```bash
# 1) frontend assets -> public/assets/
pnpm install
pnpm exec vite build

# 2) backend binary  (pure-Go SQLite, no gcc)
#    Linux/macOS:
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o gitea .
#    Windows (PowerShell):
$env:CGO_ENABLED=0; go build -buildmode=exe -o gitea.exe .
```

> The first backend compile takes a few minutes and produces a ~100+ MB binary. Later builds are fast.

---

## 4. Run (SQLite, zero config)

Just start the web server from the repo root and let the built-in installer set everything up:

```bash
# Linux/macOS:
./gitea web
# Windows:
./gitea.exe web
```

Then open **http://localhost:3000** and you'll see the **Install** page:

1. **Database Type:** choose **SQLite3** (the default path is fine).
2. Leave the rest at defaults for local dev.
3. Expand **Administrator Account Settings** and create your admin username / password / email
   (do this now so you don't have to register separately).
4. Click **Install Gitea**.

That's it — you now have a running Gitea with a SQLite database at `data/gitea.db`. Log in with the
admin account you just created.

> **Port already in use?** If something else owns `:3000`, start Gitea on another port:
> `./gitea web --port 3030` and open http://localhost:3030 instead.

### On macOS
The same `./gitea web` command works — a few Mac-specific notes:

- **Firewall prompt:** the first launch may ask *"Do you want the application `gitea` to accept
  incoming network connections?"* — click **Allow** (it's the binary you just built).
- **`permission denied`:** make the binary executable first: `chmod +x gitea`.
- **Gatekeeper "cannot be opened" warning:** only affects binaries downloaded from a browser, not
  ones you built yourself. If you ever run a downloaded release binary instead, clear the
  quarantine flag: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./gitea`.
- **Apple Silicon (M1–M4):** fully supported — Go produces a native arm64 binary, nothing extra to do.

### Live-reload while developing (optional)
If you have `make`:
```bash
make watch          # rebuilds frontend + backend on file changes (uses air)
```

---

## 5. Try it out

Create a repository (with "Initialize repository"), open an issue, push a branch, and open a pull
request so you can see the code-review UI. These are the areas most course tasks touch:

- **Code review UI** — the diff viewer and PR review flow.
- **Issues / Kanban** — issue tracking and project boards.
- **CI / Actions** — the built-in Actions runner and workflow UI.

---

## 6. Running the tests

Gitea's test suite is validated on **Linux CI**. Run it on Linux, macOS, WSL2, or the provided
`.devcontainer` — **not native Windows**, where a handful of unit tests fail for platform reasons
(symlink semantics, temp-file cleanup) rather than real bugs.

```bash
# unit tests
CGO_ENABLED=0 go test ./...
# or, with make:
make test-backend         # unit tests
make test-integration     # integration tests (defaults to SQLite via GITEA_TEST_DATABASE)
```

Frontend tests:
```bash
pnpm exec vitest run
```

---

## 7. Common gotchas

- **`git` not found at runtime:** Gitea runs git commands for every repo operation. Make sure `git`
  is on your `PATH`, not just in your IDE.
- **`go build` is slow the first time:** normal — it compiles ~3000 packages once, then caches.
- **Don't commit build artifacts:** `gitea`/`gitea.exe`, `data/`, `custom/`, and `public/assets/*`
  are gitignored. Keep them out of your commits.
- **Windows line endings:** the repo expects LF. Your editor/`.gitattributes` should keep it that way.

---

---

## Contributing workflow

All team members have write access to this repository, so the team uses a **branch-based** workflow — not forks. Here is the background and the commands.

**Why not forks?** Forking is the standard model for contributing to open-source projects where you _don't_ have write access: you fork to your own GitHub account, clone your fork, and open a PR from your fork back to the original. You will encounter this when contributing to the upstream project. But for your course team — where everyone has write access to the shared repo — it just adds confusion: two clones on your machine, two remotes to keep in sync, merge conflicts that are harder to reason about.

**Branch-based workflow** is what most professional teams use internally. You clone the shared repo once, create a short-lived branch for each issue, push the branch back to the same repo, and open a PR from that branch into `main`. One clone, one remote, full PR workflow.

### For each issue you work on

```bash
# One-time setup: clone the team repo (skip if already done)
git clone https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea.git
cd gitea

# Before starting each issue: make sure you are on a fresh main
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Create a branch named for the issue
git checkout -b feat/issue-17-dark-mode      # new feature
git checkout -b fix/issue-42-toast-dismiss   # bug fix

# ... make your changes, run tests ...

# Stage and commit
git add <the files you changed>
git commit -m "feat: add dark mode toggle (#17)"

# Push the branch to the team repo
git push origin feat/issue-17-dark-mode
```

After pushing, GitHub shows a **"Compare & pull request"** banner on the repository page. Click it to open a PR from your branch into `main`. Fill in the description (what changed and why), reference the issue (`Closes #17`), and request a review from a teammate.

**Branch naming:**

| Prefix | Use for |
|---|---|
| `feat/issue-<N>-short-description` | new features |
| `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` | bug fixes |
| `chore/short-description` | docs, config, dependency updates |

> ⚠️ **`main` is protected — direct pushes are blocked.** All changes go through a reviewed PR. If you accidentally commit to `main` locally, move your changes to a branch before pushing:
>
> ```bash
> git checkout -b fix/issue-42-my-fix   # create branch from your current state
> git checkout main
> git reset --hard origin/main          # revert local main to match remote
> ```

**After your PR is merged**, delete the branch to keep the repo tidy:

```bash
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-17-dark-mode
```

📚 **Official documentation:** <https://docs.gitea.com/> — usage, administration, and development
guides.

Gitea has its own established contribution processes. They are **not restated here** — you are
responsible for finding, reading, and following them from the sources below:

```
</details></tool-use>

## Introduction
## AI Contribution Policy

Contributions made with the assistance of AI tools are welcome, but contributors must use them responsibly and disclose that use clearly.

1. Review AI-generated code closely before marking a pull request ready for review.
2. Manually test the changes and add appropriate automated tests where feasible.
3. Only use AI to assist in contributions that you understand well enough to explain, defend, and revise yourself during review.
4. Disclose AI-assisted content clearly.
5. Do not use AI to reply to questions about your issue or pull request. The questions are for you, not an AI model.
6. AI may be used to help draft issues and pull requests, but contributors remain responsible for the accuracy, completeness, and intent of what they submit.

Maintainers reserve the right to close pull requests and issues that do not disclose AI assistance, that appear to be low-quality AI-generated content, or where the contributor cannot explain or defend the proposed changes themselves.

We welcome new contributors, but cannot sustain the effort of supporting contributors who primarily defer to AI rather than engaging substantively with the review process.

## What the repo is

`Gitea/` is a **course fork of Gitea** (CSCI 435 Software Engineering) — `origin` is `https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea.git`, branch `main`. It's upstream Gitea plus five course-authored commits layered on top:

## The only three Sprint 0 mentions

All in `Gitea/ai-logs/README.md`:

> This folder contains AI interaction logs for **each sprint**.
> See the [**Sprint 0 deliverables**](../../docs/sprints.md#d4--ai-tooling-setup) for full instructions on capturing and submitting AI logs.

That link tells you the most: **Sprint 0 has numbered deliverables, and D4 is "AI Tooling Setup."** So there are at least D1–D4, and submitting AI logs is D4.

## The structure you're expected to fill

Two parallel per-sprint trees, both currently empty (`.gitkeep` only, `sprint0` through `sprint4`):

```
ai-logs/sprint0/<your-github-username>/
    YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-description>.md
    YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-description>/     ← attachments (images, etc.)

docs/sprint0/          ← empty, no README explaining it
```

Note the logs are **per-student** (your GitHub username), not per-team. Allowed tool identifiers in the filename are fixed: `claude-code`, `claude-web`, `claude-desktop`, `cursor`, `gemini-cli`, `codex-cli`, `copilot`, `chatgpt`, `gemini-web`, `other-<name>`. For this session that's `claude-code`, so a file today would be `ai-logs/sprint0/<username>/2026-09-02_claude-code_<description>.md`.

## ⚠️ The broken link

`../../docs/sprints.md` resolves to **one level above the repo root** — outside the repository. There is no `docs/sprints.md`, and `git log --all` shows it has **never existed in this repo's history**. So either the path is a typo for `docs/sprints.md` (a file the instructor hasn't pushed yet), or the sprint spec lives outside the repo entirely — Canvas/Blackboard, a course site, or your lecture PDFs. Since the folder scaffolding landed Aug 31 and the semester just started, "not pushed yet" is the likely explanation. **Worth a `git pull` before you rely on this, and worth asking about if it's still missing.**

## What Sprint 0 is almost certainly about

`STUDENTS.md` (the guide that shipped in the same commit) reads exactly like a Sprint 0 onboarding checklist, so its contents are your best proxy for D1–D3:

1. **Toolchain + build** — Go 1.26.4+, Node 22.18+, pnpm 11+, Git. `make build`, or `pnpm install && pnpm exec vite build` then `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build`. No gcc needed — pure-Go SQLite driver, which is why it's painless on Windows.
2. **Run it** — `./gitea.exe web` → http://localhost:3000 → SQLite3 → create your admin account. Then create a repo, open an issue, open a PR to see the review UI.
3. **Contributing workflow** — **branch-based, not forks.** Everyone has write access; `main` is protected, direct pushes blocked. Branch as `feat/issue-<N>-desc`, `fix/issue-<N>-desc`, or `chore/desc`; PR into `main` with `Closes #17`; request a teammate's review.
4. **AI tooling (= D4)** — set up your AI tool and log your interactions. Two policies bind here: `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s AI Contribution Policy (disclose AI use; only submit code you can explain and defend; don't let AI answer review questions), and `AGENTS.md`, which requires an `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer on commits and **explicitly forbids `Co-Authored-By` and `Signed-off-by` trailers** — sign-off must be human.

One practical flag: that last rule conflicts with my default commit attribution, which appends `Co-Authored-By: Claude`. If you have me commit in this repo, I'll use `Assisted-by:` instead and drop the `Co-Authored-By` line, per `AGENTS.md`.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-02 20:20:38Z)**_

Saved as a standing rule. Two things now enforce it, and honestly the second is the stronger one:

1. **Memory** — recalled when I work in this project directory.
2. **The repo itself** — `Gitea/CLAUDE.md` is literally `@AGENTS.md`, so those rules load automatically for any session working in that tree. That's project-local and doesn't depend on my memory being recalled, which makes it the more reliable of the two.

Where I'd stop short of "no matter what": both mechanisms are *me reading instructions and complying*. That's reliable, not infallible — a session where memory doesn't surface and the harness default is loud is the realistic failure mode. So I'd rather not sell you a guarantee I can't structurally back.

**If you want it actually guaranteed, use a `commit-msg` hook** — git rejects the commit regardless of what I or any teammate's AI tool does:

```bash
cat > .git/hooks/commit-msg <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
if grep -qiE '^(Co-Authored-By|Signed-off-by):' "$1"; then
  echo "BLOCKED: AGENTS.md forbids Co-Authored-By / Signed-off-by trailers." >&2
  echo "Use: Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION" >&2
  exit 1
fi
EOF
chmod +x .git/hooks/commit-msg
```

That's ~10 seconds of setup and it can't forget. Note it's local-only (`.git/hooks` isn't tracked), so it protects your clone, not your teammates'. Want me to add it?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-02 20:21:42Z)**_

It's short — 21 bullets, no prose. Note `Gitea/CLAUDE.md` contains nothing but `@AGENTS.md`, so this file *is* the agent guidance for the repo.

**Build & test commands**
- `make help` lists available development targets
- `make fmt` formats `.go` files; `make lint-go` lints them
- `make lint-js` lints `.ts` files
- `make tidy` after any `go.mod` change
- Single Go test: `go test -run '^TestName$' ./modulepath/`
- Single JS test file: `pnpm exec vitest <path-filter>`
- Single Playwright e2e file: `GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='<filepath>' make test-e2e`

**Testing philosophy**
- Prefer unit tests over integration tests when logic is testable in isolation
- Aim for sub-2s local runtime for integration and e2e tests

**Code style**
- Add the current year to the copyright header of new `.go` files
- No trailing whitespace in edited files
- Preserve existing comments — don't remove or rewrite ones still relevant
- Keep comments short, prefer same-line, explain *why*, never narrate code
- TypeScript: use `!` (non-null assertion) rather than `?.`/`??` when a value is known to exist
- CSS: prefer `flex-*` helpers over per-child `tw-ml-*`/`tw-mr-*` margins; fall back to `tw-*` utilities when specificity needs `!important`

**Git & PR conventions**
- Conventional Commits for messages and PR titles: `type(scope): subject`, `!` before the colon if breaking; `test` type for test-only changes
- Never force-push, amend, or squash unless asked — use new commits and normal push to update a PR
- Include authorship attribution in issue and PR comments
- Always add `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION`
- Never add `Co-Authored-By` or `Signed-off-by` — sign-off must be done by a human

Two of these are in tension with your setup, worth knowing before you hit them:

- **It assumes `make` exists.** Seven of the 21 bullets are `make` targets, and you opted to skip `make`. The no-make equivalents work fine (`go test -run ...` and `pnpm exec vitest` are already make-free; `make fmt` ≈ `gofmt -w`, `make tidy` ≈ `go mod tidy`), but `make lint-go` wraps golangci-lint with the repo's config and is more annoying to replicate by hand. Say the word if you want `make` after all.
- **`make test-e2e` uses shell env-var syntax** (`GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='...' make ...`), which won't run in PowerShell — and per `STUDENTS.md` the suite is Linux-validated anyway, so that one belongs in WSL2 or the devcontainer regardless.

Confirmed — `make` from PowerShell fails hard (exit -1): it uses `cmd.exe` as the shell, so `sed` is missing and Windows' `FIND`/`find` collide with the POSIX ones the Makefile expects.

**So: run `make` from Git Bash, not PowerShell.** I'd avoid "fixing" this by putting Git's `usr\bin` on your global PATH — that shadows Windows' `find`, `sort`, and friends with POSIX versions and breaks unrelated things.

Found a real problem — and it's the kind that would quietly pollute your PRs all semester.

**`make fmt` under Go 1.27 reformats a file that upstream considers correctly formatted.** It rewrote 12 lines of `modules/git/key.go` (re-indenting multi-value composite-literal returns). I reverted it; your tree is clean again.

The cause:

- `go.mod` declares `go 1.26.4`, and CI resolves its Go from that file (`go-version-file: go.mod` in `.github/actions/go-setup/action.yml`) → **CI runs Go 1.26.x**
- winget only offers **1.27.0**, which is what I installed — gofmt's rules changed between those versions

Your build is unaffected (1.27 compiled it fine). But `AGENTS.md` tells you to run `make fmt` before committing, and doing that on 1.27 stages unrelated churn in files you never touched — exactly what gets flagged in review.

Cache warming for `GOOS=linux` (note `WARM_EXIT` uses `PIPESTATUS` this time, so it reports the real status).

**Meanwhile, this is the higher-leverage fix — Defender exclusions for the Go caches.** Go's build cache is millions of tiny files, and real-time scanning each one is the classic reason Go is slow on Windows. Run this to add them:

```
! powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Start-Process powershell -Verb RunAs -Wait -ArgumentList '-NoProfile','-Command','Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath \"C:\Users\carso\go\",\"C:\Users\carso\AppData\Local\go-build\",\"C:\Program Files\Go\"; Write-Host Done; Start-Sleep 3'"
```

That excludes only your Go toolchain, module cache, and build cache — not your documents or downloads.

**Honest framing on where this is heading:** `make fmt`, `go build`, and the frontend all work fine natively. `make lint-go` is the one target that fights Windows, because it cross-compiles the whole tree to Linux. Even warmed, expect it to be slow-ish. Given `STUDENTS.md` already says the test suite must run on Linux, **the durable answer for both linting and testing is WSL2 or the repo's `.devcontainer`** — native Windows stays great for build/run/iterate.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-03 15:45:21Z)**_

<tool-use data-tool-type="generic" data-tool-name="AskUserQuestion"><details>

**Where should the repo live for WSL linting/testing? WSL2's access to Windows drives (/mnt/c) is slow — that's the whole reason lint failed natively.**

Options:
- **Fresh clone inside WSL at ~/gitea (Recommended)** - Clone into the Linux filesystem (ext4), where I/O is fast. This is what makes lint and tests actually usable. Costs ~350 MB and gives you two working copies — you'd sync them by pushing/pulling through GitHub, which fits the branch-based workflow the course already requires. Best paired with VS Code's WSL extension so you edit directly in Linux.
- **Use the existing Windows clone via /mnt/c** - One clone, one source of truth, nothing to sync. But every file read crosses the WSL/Windows boundary, and lint was already too slow natively — this may well reproduce the same problem rather than fix it.
- **Set it up, but leave the clone for later** - Finish installing the WSL toolchain (Go, Node, pnpm, make) and stop there. You decide the clone question when you actually need to lint or test.


**Answer:** just follow the directions for how to set everything up. make sure my setup is exactly like that, you can restart if needed.". Read the answers carefully — they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed — and follow what they actually say.

**Yes — all of it stays.** Your configuration lives on this machine's filesystem, not in your Claude account.

Your status line is `~/.claude/settings.json` pointing at `~/.claude/statusline.ps1` (a 3.3 KB PowerShell script you wrote). Both are plain files on disk. Logging out doesn't touch them.

**Survives a logout / account switch — everything in `~/.claude/`:**

| | |
|---|---|
| `statusline.ps1` + the `statusLine` config | ✅ your status line |
| `settings.json` | model `opus[1m]`, theme, permissions, notifications |
| `settings.local.json` | machine-local overrides |
| `CLAUDE.md` | your global instructions (the "Machine: SCHOOL" file) |
| `projects/` | including all the Gitea memory I saved today |
| `history.jsonl`, `sessions/`, `file-history/` | past conversations |
| `plugins/`, `chrome/` | installed extras |

**The only thing tied to your account is `.credentials.json`** — logging out rewrites that one file and nothing else.

**What *does* change with a different account** isn't config, it's entitlements:

- **Model access.** Your settings request `opus[1m]` (Opus with the 1M context window). If the other account is on a plan without it, Claude Code falls back to whatever that plan allows — the setting stays written, it just can't be honored.
- **Usage limits** reset to the new account's quota.
- **Anything server-side** — artifacts you've published, cloud sessions — belongs to the account that created it, so those won't follow you.

If you want a safety net before switching, `~/.claude/settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `statusline.ps1` are the four files worth copying somewhere. I can back them up if you'd like — though a logout genuinely shouldn't disturb them.
